title: Protection & Discrimination Basics
objective: Develop practical awareness of protection coordination, discrimination/selectivity and the information needed to review protective-device decisions without overstepping engineering approval boundaries.

learn.heading: What senior designers should understand
bullets: Protection decisions depend on system topology, fault levels, equipment ratings, load characteristics and the required coordination philosophy.
Discrimination/selectivity aims to limit unnecessary upstream operation when a downstream fault occurs.
Device settings and ratings are controlled engineering information and must not be guessed from appearance or habit.
SLDs, schedules and equipment data must remain consistent with the approved protection design.
When detailed short-circuit or coordination analysis is required, document the interface and obtain the responsible engineer's result.
learn.takeaway: Senior drafting/design readiness includes understanding what protection coordination is trying to achieve and how to document it safely and traceably.

apply.scenario: A fictional LV distribution system has an incomer breaker, a motor feeder and two final circuits. The project requires a basic coordination review record, but detailed fault calculations are supplied separately by an engineer.
tasks: Draw a simplified protection hierarchy showing upstream and downstream devices.
Create a coordination input checklist covering device type, rating, settings, fault level and downstream equipment requirements.
Review a fictional set of device data and flag one obvious inconsistency between a schedule and the SLD.
Write three questions you would send to the responsible engineer before finalising protection information.
Define what evidence should be retained with the drawing package.
apply.deliverable: A sanitized protection hierarchy and coordination review checklist with identified interfaces and discrepancies.

questions.q: What is the basic purpose of discrimination/selectivity?
a: Make every breaker trip at the same time.
Prefer the appropriate downstream protective device to operate for a downstream fault where the coordination design permits.
Eliminate the need for fault studies.
questions.why: Selectivity is intended to limit unnecessary upstream interruption.

questions.q: A protective-device setting is missing from the approved information. What should you do?
a: Flag the missing controlled input and obtain the approved setting before documenting it as final.
Copy a setting from another project.

questions.q: A drawing and schedule show different breaker ratings. What is the strongest response?
a: Record the discrepancy, trace the controlled source and correct the affected records after verification.
Leave both values because the engineer will notice eventually.
questions.why: Cross-document discrepancies must be visible and resolved against controlled information.

check.passRule: Explain the coordination intent and identify the information that must come from approved engineering analysis.

evidence.prompt: Capture a sanitized protection hierarchy, coordination checklist or discrepancy review showing your understanding of protection design boundaries.

integration.home: Recommend Week 11 after completion and show protection coordination awareness as the latest milestone.
integration.journal: Reflect on what protection decisions you can confidently document and what requires specialist engineering analysis.
integration.portfolio: Add the protection review artefact as evidence of coordinated electrical design awareness.
